title: Fabrication-free assessment of microwave losses in germanium-based dielectrics and superconductors
authors: Haoran Lu, Kushagra Aggarwal, Xiangqin Wang, Pauline Drexler, Daniel Tong, Maciej W. Olszewski, Anand Ithepalli, Lingda Kong, Debdeep Jena, Peter L. McMahon, David A. Muller, Dominique Bougeard, Valla Fatemi
abstract: We present a flip-chip-based sensing scheme to measure effective microwave losses associated with target materials for quantum technologies, without requiring any device fabrication on the material under test. Using this approach, we quantify the microwave losses of a strain-engineered Ge/SiGe quantum well heterostructure and investigate losses arising from its Ge substrate and intermediate layers. The quality factors of the fabricated microwave resonators agree with the losses of dielectric materials independently extracted from flip-chip sensing measurements. We further study the superconductor platinum silicon germanide (PtSiGe) prepared by thermal reaction with a deposited Pt film, finding high microwave losses that limit the suitability of the films studied here as the sole superconductor for high-quality resonator applications. By coating Pt with Nb prior to the reaction, we observe a substantial reduction in microwave loss and a nearly three-fold enhancement of the transport critical temperature. The temperature dependence of the microwave loss is consistent with gap inhomogeneity in both superconducting films. These results identify constraints on material choices, provide design guidance for microwave circuits on planar Ge heterostructures, and demonstrate a fast-turnaround testing method for new materials for superconducting quantum circuits.
summary: This work presents a novel, fabrication-free microwave sensing technique using a flip-chip setup to quantify microwave losses in materials for quantum devices. The authors successfully applied this to measure losses in Ge/SiGe dielectrics and superconducting films like PtSiGe. This method provides critical material constraints and design guidance for building high-quality superconducting quantum circuits.
main_problem: To develop a fabrication-free method to accurately measure effective microwave losses in novel materials intended for quantum technologies, specifically dielectrics and superconductors.
main_result: The technique successfully quantified losses in Ge/SiGe heterostructures and showed that coating PtSiGe with Nb significantly reduced microwave loss and enhanced the critical temperature.
method: A flip-chip-based sensing scheme is employed where a microwave resonator placed over the target material measures the material's participation ratio for both dielectric and superconducting losses.
model_or_system: The platform involves a microwave resonator sensor chip placed on top of the material under test (e.g., Ge/SiGe or PtSiGe) via pogo pins, allowing for non-destructive, in-situ loss measurement.
key_observables: Participation ratio (pr_material, pr_MA), microwave loss tangents ($\delta$), and the temperature dependence of microwave loss.
important_parameters: Low-photon and high-photon microwave regimes, strain engineering parameters in Ge/SiGe, and the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the measured loss is dominated by the target material's intrinsic properties and that the sensing setup accurately isolates the material's contribution.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the flip-chip sensing schematics for both dielectric and superconducting loss measurement, showing how participation ratios are calculated and how material losses vary with geometry.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the sensing scheme, applies it to characterize dielectric losses in Ge/SiGe, then extends the method to measure superconducting losses in PtSiGe, concluding with design guidance and material constraints.
why_interesting: The development of a non-destructive, rapid characterization tool for superconducting and dielectric losses is crucial for advancing superconducting quantum circuit design, bridging materials science and quantum engineering.
